newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian court orders Rao cases to safer location.
newsitem.headline: Indian court orders Rao cases to safer location.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao won a small victory in his legal struggle on Friday when the Supreme Court ordered hearings in two criminal cases moved from a crowded court to a more secure site.
Rao has been ordered to appear on two days next week to face charges in separate cases, one alleging criminal conspiracy to cheat and the other criminal forgery.
It was not immediately clear whether the Supreme Court's ruling would force a postponement in the hearings.
Rao, who has round-the-clock bodyguards with machineguns, and Delhi police had argued he could be attacked if he appeared at the sprawling Tis Hazari court where the hearings were planned.

Police cited Kashmiri and Sikh extremists, saying they could penetrate the Tis Hazari courts and launch an attack on Rao, 75, who resigned as prime minister in May after his Congress Party suffered a humiliating general election defeat.
Rao, who was prime minister at a time when militancy peaked in Kashmir, would have to give up his special bodyguards once he entered the Tis Hazari courts.
Authorities suggested the hearings be held in a cavernous, marble-walled conference centre, with easily controlled access and where hundreds of journalists could be accommodated.
Rao would be the first prime minister or former prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges.

An appearance by Rao at the grimy Tis Hazari courts, which handle even petty offences, could have proved an embarrassment for the former prime minister, who rarely ventures outside his heavily-guarded New Delhi home.
The Supreme Court told Delhi police to indicate where the hearings, one set for next Monday and the other for Wednesday, could be held to ensure Rao's safety.
The two-judge bench said Rao was exempted from having to appear in court until a new venue was chosen.
Rao has been summoned to appear in court next Monday to face charges in a 13-year-old case of criminal conspiracy to cheat.
He denies allegations that he helped a Hindu guru cheat an expatriate businessman of $100,000 in 1983.
Rao has also been ordered to appear next Wednesday in a separate case of criminal forgery dating from 1989.
On Wednesday, Rao was briefly arrested at home then quickly released on interim bail in the forgery case.
Delhi chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar was scheduled to rule later on Friday on a request by Rao to be exempted from appearing at next Wednesday's hearing.
Rao's lawyers told the court on Thursday their client could be attacked by militants and should not be required to appear personally in court in the forgery case.
His counsel also asked the court to extend the temporary bail, which a judge granted Rao in the case earlier this week.
The lawyers said Rao suffers from diabetes and heart problems and needs round-the-clock medical supervision.
The ruling marked the latest chapter in a legal saga which has forced Rao to step down as Congress leader and rocked the balance of power between his party and the government.
He quit in disgrace as Congress leader last month after a judge upheld the summons ordering him to appear in court.
Fallout from the cases has affected relations between Congress and Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition, which depends on Congress' support to survive.
Some left-wing leaders have accused Deve Gowda of shielding Rao from the full brunt of the law.
But some Rao loyalists have accused the government of manoeuvring to bring down Rao, who remains leader of Congress's parliamentary delegation.
